name: Keycloak
summary: An identity and access management server that isolates users and credentials in realms, executes configurable authentication flows, and issues protocol tokens for clients and services.

features.name: Realm-isolated identity model
features.description: A realm manages its own users, credentials, roles, groups, clients, and sessions; users belong to and authenticate within a realm boundary.
benefits: Provides a tenant and administration boundary for identity state
costs: Cross-realm administration and shared deployment concerns remain separate from realm data

features.name: Configurable authentication and brokering flows
features.description: Keycloak represents login as configurable flows with authenticators, required actions, identity-provider brokering, and federation providers.
benefits: Supports password, passkey, OTP, external IdP, and federation strategies
costs: Flow ordering and provider failures create many authentication states

features.name: Client-scoped token and assertion issuance
features.description: Clients request authentication and tokens; protocol mappers, client scopes, roles, and sessions shape signed OIDC tokens or SAML assertions.
benefits: Separates application integration from user credential handling
costs: Token contents and authorization meaning depend on client and mapper configuration

mathematical_views.question: How are users, groups, roles, clients, sessions, and identity providers connected within isolated realms?
assumptions: Realm membership is a boundary on user and client management
Role and group mappings are typed edges
The graph abstracts persistence and administrative authorization details

mathematical_views.question: Which authenticator, required action, broker, or federation transition leads a login session to success or failure?
assumptions: A flow is an ordered conditional sequence
External identity or credential checks may fail or require additional actions
The view does not infer security strength from flow topology alone

mathematical_views.question: How do session identity, roles, scopes, and protocol mappers project into a client-specific token or assertion?
assumptions: Token claims are selected by client and protocol configuration
Tokens are signed outputs of an authenticated session
The model abstracts cryptographic algorithm and key rotation details

costs: Realm proliferation and cross-realm administration increase configuration overhead
Flexible flow graphs enlarge the failure and review surface
Mappers and scopes can make authorization behavior difficult to inspect globally
